The Mexican Social Security Institute (IMSS) insures about 22 million workers against work risks:
work accidents, commuting accidents and occupational diseases. It publishes the cases it handles
each year in its statistical yearbook. This notebook uses national figures from 2011 to 2024 and
detailed tables from 2016 to 2024: state offices, economic activities, age and sex, occupational
diseases, causes of accidents, injured body regions and occupations. Read the module
[README](../README.md) and [data dictionary](../data_dictionary.md) first.

**How to use this notebook**

- Run each code chunk in order (the green arrow in RStudio, or Ctrl/Cmd + Shift + Enter).
- Answer the questions under each **Your answer** heading.
- When you are done, click **Knit** to produce an HTML report to submit.

# Part 0. Load the data

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(forcats)

base <- "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/eddiekasner/occupational-safety-health-datasets/main/modules/mx-imss-work-risks/data"
read_module <- function(folder, name, ...) {
  local <- file.path("..", "data", folder, name)
  read_csv(if (file.exists(local)) local else file.path(base, folder, name), show_col_types = FALSE,
           ...)
}

# National companies, workers, cases, permanent incapacities and deaths, 2011 to 2024
national <- read_module("tidy", "national.csv")
# The same by IMSS state office, and cases by economic activity and by age and sex, 2016 to 2024
by_state <- read_module("tidy", "by_state.csv")
by_activity <- read_module("tidy", "by_activity.csv")
by_age_sex <- read_module("tidy", "by_age_sex.csv")
# Occupational diseases by diagnosis, 2011 to 2024
diseases <- read_module("tidy", "occupational_diseases.csv")
# Accidents by cause, by body region and type of injury, and by occupation
causes <- read_module("tidy", "accident_causes.csv")
body <- read_module("tidy", "body_region_injury.csv")
occupations <- read_module("tidy", "occupations.csv")

# Workers each year, to compute rates
workers <- national |> filter(measure == "Workers") |> select(year, workers = value)
```

Mexican law counts **commuting accidents** (on the way between home and work) as work risks.
Cases are counted in the year they **end** (medical discharge, permanent incapacity or death).
Only workers insured by IMSS are covered: mostly private-sector employees in formal jobs.

# Part 1. National trends

```{r trends}
national |>
  filter(measure == "Cases",
         risk %in% c("Work accidents", "Commuting accidents", "Occupational diseases")) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, value, colour = risk)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(title = "Work risk cases accepted by IMSS", x = NULL, y = "Cases", colour = NULL)

national |>
  filter(measure %in% c("Cases", "Deaths"), risk == "Work accidents") |>
  select(year, measure, value) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = measure, values_from = value) |>
  left_join(workers, by = "year") |>
  mutate(cases_per_100_workers = round(100 * Cases / workers, 2),
         deaths_per_100000_workers = round(1e5 * Deaths / workers, 1))
```

**Questions**

1. How did the number of insured workers and the work accident rate per 100 workers change from
   2011 to 2024? Was the number of work accidents rising or falling?
2. Work accidents and commuting accidents both dropped in 2020. Commuting accidents then rose to a
   new high, and work accidents almost returned to their 2011 level. Suggest reasons for the drop
   and the rebound.
3. The death rate from work accidents was lowest in 2021 and 2022. Before concluding that work got
   safer, what other explanations would you check?

# Part 2. COVID-19 as an occupational disease

```{r covid}
diseases |>
  filter(disease %in% c("Total", "COVID-19", "COVID-19-related respiratory diseases")) |>
  select(year, disease, cases) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = disease, values_from = cases, values_fill = 0) |>
  mutate(excluding_covid = Total - `COVID-19` - `COVID-19-related respiratory diseases`)

by_state |>
  filter(office == "National", year %in% 2020:2023,
         risk %in% c("COVID-19", "Occupational diseases excluding COVID-19")) |>
  select(year, risk, cases, deaths)
```

**Questions**

1. How many occupational disease cases were COVID-19 in 2020, and what share of occupational
   disease deaths? Which workers do you think made up most of these cases?
2. For COVID-19 to count as an occupational disease, the infection must be linked to work. What
   makes that link hard to establish for an infectious disease that is also spreading in the
   community?
3. If you wanted a trend in occupational disease from 2011 to 2024, how would you handle 2020 to
   2023? (Look at the README for the 2022 revision too.)

# Part 3. Who gets hurt

```{r age-sex}
by_age_sex |>
  filter(year == 2024, workers > 1000) |>
  mutate(cases_per_100 = 100 * cases / workers) |>
  ggplot(aes(age_group, cases_per_100, fill = sex)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  labs(title = "Work risks per 100 insured workers by age and sex, 2024",
       subtitle = "All work risks, including commuting accidents and occupational diseases",
       x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))

by_age_sex |>
  group_by(year, sex) |>
  summarise(cases_per_100 = round(100 * sum(cases) / sum(workers), 2), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = sex, values_from = cases_per_100)
```

**Questions**

1. Which age groups have the highest rate? Why might young workers be at higher risk?
2. Men had the higher rate until 2018, the rates were equal in 2019, and women have had the higher
   rate since 2020. Using Part 2, suggest one reason. What other data would help you check it?

**Your answer:**



# Part 4. Industries and states

```{r industries}
by_activity |>
  filter(year == 2024, risk == "Work accidents", activity != "National", !is.na(workers)) |>
  mutate(per_100 = 100 * cases / workers) |>
  ggplot(aes(per_100, fct_reorder(activity, per_100))) +
  geom_col() +
  labs(title = "Work accidents per 100 insured workers, 2024", x = NULL, y = NULL)

by_state |>
  filter(year == 2024, risk == "Work accidents", office != "National") |>
  mutate(per_100 = round(100 * cases / workers, 2),
         deaths_per_100000 = round(1e5 * deaths / workers, 1)) |>
  arrange(desc(per_100)) |>
  select(office, workers, cases, per_100, deaths, deaths_per_100000)
```

**Questions**

1. Which division of economic activity has the highest work accident rate? Is it the one with the
   most accidents?
2. The work accident rate varies about threefold between state offices. Give two reasons that are
   about reporting or coverage rather than about safety.

# Part 5. How accidents happen

```{r causes}
causes |>
  filter(year == 2024) |>
  group_by(risk, cause) |>
  summarise(cases = sum(cases), .groups = "drop_last") |>
  mutate(share = round(cases / sum(cases), 3)) |>
  slice_max(cases, n = 5)

body |>
  filter(year == 2024) |>
  group_by(body_region, injury) |>
  summarise(cases = sum(cases), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(injury, fct_reorder(body_region, cases, .fun = sum), fill = cases)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(title = "Work accidents by body region and type of injury, 2024", x = NULL, y = NULL,
       fill = "Cases") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

**Questions**

1. What are the most common causes of work accidents, and of commuting accidents?
2. Which combination of body region and type of injury is most common? Name two controls that
   would prevent it.
3. "Exposure to inanimate mechanical forces" covers being struck by, caught in or cut by objects
   and machinery. Why is it a less useful category for prevention than, say, "Falls"?
